results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 38 aligned units: the outliner's summary states the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to, in the spec's order (p01-p02, p03-p05, p06-p12, p13/p14/p27/p15, p16-p18, p19-p21, p22-p23, p24-p26, p28/p29/p31/p30, p32-p33, p34-p38). The three callouts match nothing, by page format.

Three units were marked two_ideas; none fails. Introduction ¶2 states thesis and roadmap by design (p02). Where the Sources Disagree ¶3 gives the book's resolution and the one difference of degree it leaves, which is a qualification of the same position and is what p26 declares. Checklist ¶2 closes the part and hands off to Part IV by design (p38, last chapter of its part).

Every body unit serves the supporting claims its section declares: scene and anti-patterns S5; two spaces and handover S1/S2; discovery S3; product operations S4; sources S2/S5; worked example S1-S4; AI S2/S3. No unit is off the thesis.

Figure 1 has a caption saying what it shows; each of the three tables has a lead-in saying what it gives (and the first has two following paragraphs on its hard rows); each quotation (Perri on transparency, Perri and Tilles on enablement, Foster and Nerlikar twice) is followed or framed by a sentence saying what it shows; the Corvane scenarios end on a stated point (the shared missing line, the Escalation Ladder, the leaders judging a missed target).

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary and picks up the declared known information, e.g. 'This chapter draws that line.' (p02), 'The Reporting team had the opposite experience.' (p05), 'A handover of this kind is the default, and two conditions move the line' (p27), 'Discovery needs customers and data, and both move out of a team's reach' (product-operations), 'Each of those two sides has a school behind it' (sources), 'Replacing the block meant changing a scheduling rule, and that decision was not yet the team's.' (p31), 'With the rule in its own hands' (p30). In What AI Changes ¶1 and Checklist ¶2 the declared relationship arrives in the second sentence or later in the paragraph, after a house-format opener; accepted.

results.finding: Reported by both flow readers (A item 1, B item 3), both rated (b): this sentence and the next explain rows of the settings table before the table is shown, so they could be mapped only after reading the table; B adds that naming a solution and promising a date read as different things. Not corroborated as a blocking point because neither reader rated it (a). Local fix: move the two sentences after the table.

results.quote: By 2025 she was the CPO of about 500 people, and every rule question still waited for her.

Terms new to the book's reader are glossed at first use (empowered product team, feature team, problem space, solution space, decision right, backlog, key results, guardrails, discovery, delivery, known unknowns, product operations, the waiter, The Feature Factory, The Escalation Ladder, rule engine); the evidence labels, the AI labels and Corvane come from the book's introduction. 'Middle horizon' and 'outcome review' are not glossed here but come from the two preceding chapters of the same part (three horizons in Roadmaps and Horizons, which this chapter links; the outcome review in Outcomes Over Output), so the book's reader has them; the flow readers' note on 'middle horizon' is recorded under flow_is_followable. A one-clause gloss would cost little.
Opens on a puzzling scenario (one announcement, two opposite results) and moves to the thesis and roadmap; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, dawn of man or book report.

The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, gives a course of action and closes the part; it does not open with 'in conclusion', does not end on a rephrased thesis alone and holds no body evidence. The engineering model in the last paragraph is the declared hand-off to Part IV, not a new subtopic.

Checklist ¶1 states what no single section states ('one arrangement seen from four sides') and Checklist ¶2 gives the so-what ('The argument between top-down and bottom-up product work dissolves once each level knows which space it owns'), with the leader's course of action carried by the eight checks.

Checklist ¶2 returns to both declared elements: 'Corvane's two teams of 2025 each held one end of that chain' and 'The forty-one features of 2024 ... were output with no outcome above it, forty-one solutions chosen outside the teams that built them.'

The introduction-only reader named the claim, all sections in order (two teams, two spaces and the sorting, three patterns, two failures, the quarrel of the sources, the worked team, AI), the kind of evidence (a running fictional case, a classification, named patterns, a reading of two schools) and the tone (plain, declarative, prescriptive, to 'you').

The cold reader's assignments equal the expected ones: leaders for (1) and (3); the team for (2) and (4); (5) jointly, leaders naming the measure and the team proposing the target; (6) the team inside engineering guardrails. The two hardest, (5) and (6), are justified from the chapter (accountability for a proposed target; a guardrail limits the choice and does not make it).

The tension is stated ('the two schools appear to disagree about where product direction comes from') and resolved explicitly ('This book's resolution follows the two books and not the two readings', followed by who owns which space and the one difference of degree that remains).

The closing paragraph synthesizes Part III: 'Outcome, vision, roadmap and empowered team are one chain. Each link says less about the solution and more about the reason', reads Corvane's two teams and the forty-one features through it, and says why it matters.

Each borrowed concept names its book and the concept (Empowered: empowered product team, feature team, key results, high-integrity commitment, four risks; Inspired: discovery and delivery; Escaping the Build Trap with Bungay's The Art of Action: intent; the waiter; Build What Matters: vision-led management, game of telephone; Product Operations: enablement function, 'process people'). Rules of thumb and extensions are marked as the author's ('My working rule, drawn from Build What Matters', 'A quicker measure, my own', 'that is my recommendation, not the book's', 'I divide product decisions into two spaces', and the 'author's synthesis' list).

Each of the three patterns names its user and an outcome measure: the handover (the product team and the leader who hands over; any member can say the problem, the measure and what the team may decide; count of items that arrived as named features), discovery and delivery (the product team; ideas dropped before building and shipped changes shown to move the measure), product operations (product managers and their teams; time from a question to the data or to a customer).
